newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China, Taiwan, HK markets volatile after Deng death.
newsitem.headline: China, Taiwan, HK markets volatile after Deng death.

text.p: Stock markets in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan turned highly volatile on Thursday, contrary to forecasts by market pundits who expected a moderate response to overnight news China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping had died.
Reaction in U.S. markets had been muted and many other Asian markets also showed little response to the news, focusing instead on domestic considerations.
Shanghai shares opened nearly all 10 percent limit-down on Thursday in reaction to Deng's death and those in Shenzhen also dropped, but both quickly rebounded.
At mid-morning, the Shanghai foreign-currency B share index was down just 0.78 percent or 0.508 points at 64.622, while the Shenzhen B index was up 0.17 percent or 0.24 points at 141.99.
Shenzhen B shares initially had lost 7.26 percent while A shares fell 9.8 percent.
"The markets have pulled back very quickly," said Alex Conroy of ING-Barings.
She said a fall followed by a rebound had long been the expected reaction to Deng's death, but added the speed of the response was surprising.
"It's happening a bit faster than I expected," she said.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index dropped 92 points, or 0.71 percent, to 13,013 in early trading, but soon reversed course and was up 106 points, or 0.81 percent, at 13,212.
In Taiwan, stocks bounced up and down. They fell 0.81 percent after surrendering early gains but recovered to rise 61.37, or 0.80 percent, to 7,718.22 in early trade.
The Taiwan dollar also fell, but was off its lows at T$27.596.
Taiwan officials moved swiftly to foster stability in its market following Deng's death.
The central bank said it will inject funds into the banking system to ensure sufficient liquidity and a government spokesman said it was prepared to support financial markets.
Market-watchers in Hong Kong had anticipated a moderate reaction and said any move was likely to be temporary.
"Probably to a large extent it has been discounted because of the rumours of the past week," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
Singapore shares weakened initially in response to the news, but traders said any impact would be limited.
The Straits Times Index hit a low of 2,236.53, before firming to 2,258.48, a rise of 11.49 points or 0.51 percent from Wednesday's close.
But in Tokyo, Deng's death failed to influence traders, who were focused on press reports the Japanese government would provide funds to help banks recoup problem loans.
The key Nikkei 225-share Index powered ahead by 413.16 points, or 2.22 percent, to end the morning session at 19,012.28.
U.S. markets showed little reaction to the news, which came while they were open.
"This news has been largely discounted over the last several years," one market economist said.

Another analyst noted that Deng already had retired from politics in 1993 and that Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin had been carefully positioned to assume the top leadership in anticipation of Deng's death.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended off 47.33 points at 7,020.13 on Wednesday.
The dollar initially rose on the news but finished off highs at 1.6980 marks and 124.55 yen, compared with 1.6855 marks and 123.85 yen, respectively, on Tuesday.
The dollar weakened slightly against the yen in early Tokyo trading, but dealers expect the currency will attract buying if it falls to 123 yen.
Taiwan's finance minister, Paul Chiu, said he did not expect Taipei's share market to plunge in reaction to Deng's death.
Australian shares opened lower in-line with the drop on Wall Street and a cautious mood ahead of the release of corporate earnings. Traders said Deng's death was not a market factor.
The All Ordinaries share index was off 13.9 points, or 0.56 percent at 2,477.1.
Similarly, in New Zealand, stocks ended off their lows, with Deng's death having no impact on trading. The market finished down 3.50 points, or 0.15 percent, at 2,325.85.
